fragments.text: Kia ora tato katoa. Thank you so much for the opportunity to join you today from Aotearoa, New Zealand, for the UNESCO AI for AI conference. The Christchurch Hall was born out of the unprecedented horror of the 2019 terrorist attacking Christchurch that killed 51 people and was livestreamed online. It was a wake-up call to the world. Today, the Christchurch Hall is a multi-stakeholder community of over 130 online platforms, governments and civil society organisations. With a clear mission to eliminate terrorist and violent extremist content online while upholding human rights and preserving a free, open and secure internet. Supporting this work is the Christchurch Hall Foundation, an independent, not-for-profit that I lead, that enables and strengthens the core community.

At its core, our work is about online safety within the broader context of internet governance and increasingly AI governance. In today's shifting geopolitical landscape, this mission is more urgent than ever. We began with a determination that the events of March 15, 2019 must never happen again. We remain active because online TVAC is not just a digital issue, it's a matter of national security, economic stability, public safety and the prevention of radicalisation, especially among the young. These are concerns shared across our diverse community and rightly so. Our work is guided by the 25 commitments of the Christchurch Hall, grouped into five key themes, all focused on eliminating terrorist and violent extremist content online. The themes are information integrity in TVAC, new technology in TVAC, gender-based violence and violent extremism, youth and radicalisation to violent extremism, offline linkages and TVAC.

Alongside these pillars, the Foundation also supports core capabilities of the core. Most notably, the ongoing development and delivery of a Christchurch Response Protocol, seeking to de-escalate after violence. The rise of new AI tools has transformed our technology landscape, bringing enormous potential, but also significant responsibility. AI can relieve the burdens of repetitive tasks, unlock creativity, a powerful shift. But we must also recognise that AI remains poorly understood by many, and that's where risks emerge. Synthetic content, especially when used to inflame divisions or distort reality as a growing concern. And yet, if harnessed responsibility frontier models and emerging tech, strengthen trust and safety tools and help protect people more effectively than ever before. The Christchurch call is committed to ensuring that AI systems, especially those used for content moderation and recommendation algorithms, are developed and deployed with safety, security and ethics at their core.

Key concerns in our domain include the amplification of harmful content. Engagement-based algorithms can unintentionally promote terrorist and violent extremist material. Bias and discrimination remain an issue. AI may reflect or reinforce societal biases, disproportionately impacting marginalized communities. Transparency remains a concern. Many models operate as black boxes, making decisions difficult to interpret or to challenge. And security vulnerabilities are a concern too. AI can be weaponised as bread disinformation, deep fakes or rather malicious content. To address these risks, we advocate for explainable AI systems in moderation and recommendation, for independent audits and impact assessments of platform AI tools. For frameworks that embed human rights, fairness and inclusion in AI design, for multi-state colder collaboration to shape ethical standards and policy development.

For safe guards to prevent AI misuse and spreading violent extremist content, for continued research into algorithmic amplification and its effects on users. For exploration of adversarial attacks and AI system resilience, for alignment with international efforts to ensure that radicalisation and violent extremism remains central to global AI governance. And above all, for ongoing dialogue across governments, tech companies, civil society and academia, focused on the intersection of new technologies and our specialist domain area. The Christchurch call believes the future of digital safety, especially around terrorist and violent extremist content, hinges on how we govern AI today right now. As AI increasingly shapes online spaces, the risks of misuse, whether through violent extremist content, algorithmic bias or opaque decision-making, require urgent coordinated action.

For championing transparency, ethical governance and global collaboration, we can ensure AI becomes a force for good and not a vector for harm. The Christchurch call community is deeply invested in this mission. Together, governments, platforms, civil society and researchers, we work to uphold the values of safety, dignity and respect online. We invite all stakeholders to join us in advancing responsible AI practices that protect communities, preserve democratic integrity and foster a safer digital future for all, with a clear focus on managing the risks and eliminating terrorist and violent extremist content online. Thank you for your time today. I hope that's been a helpful outline of the intersection between AI governance work and our mission, and I wish you all the very best for your deliberations today. Thank you very much.
